titleStmt.title: To Harriet Shaw Weaver. Monday, 6 November 1922
titleStmt.author: James Joyce

seriesStmt.p: Machine readable texts of the unpublished correspondence of James Joyce

projectDesc.p: James Joyce's unpublished correspondence, collected, annotated, and made available as a digital edition

div.p:
My eye continues to improve rapidly. To whom were press copies of the second edition sent and was it suggested to send any copies to non-press critics such as Prof. Saentsbury Saintsbury
or Dr. Brandes? Miss Beach sent me Criterion so will you please send the copy you meant for me to Mrs. Murray (group A). Mr. Larbaud’s article reads very well. It is a relief after recent criticisms to meet a man who knows what he wants to say, knows how to say it and says it. The touch (of) at the end of the second last paragraph is very neat. It will flatter English critics too as coming from a Frenchman.

postscript.p:
P.S. Errata p. 37 l.2 from foot
Divid Divide better A catalectic
join better march ing

div.note: Dr Colin’s treatment of JJ’s eyes in Nice in mid-October apparently had a healing effect. The Joyces would depart from Nice for Paris almost a week after this letter was sent (13 November 1922).

Founded by T.S. Eliot in October 1922, The Criterion ran until January 1939 as a quarterly literary review (with the exception of years 1927-28 when it ran monthly). Its inaugural issue featured Eliot’s The Waste Land and excerpts of Valery Larbaud’s 1921 lecture on Ulysses. JJ may have been reminded of Saintsbury because he had an article in the same first issue of Criterion.

Larbaud’s “The Ulysses of James Joyce”, a translated and excerpted version of his 1921 Paris lecture. The Criterion article follows the Nouvelle Revue Française’s publication of Larbaud’s lecture as its leading article on 1 April 1922.

This is the text: “The English language has a very great store of obscene words and expressions, and the author of Ulysses has enriched his book generously and boldly from this vocabulary.” Lucia deletes “(of)” by putting it between brackets.
